utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, have the witness brought in, please. (The accused/witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo -- first of all, I would like to say good morning to the interpreters, to Defence and Prosecution counsel, good morning to the witness, General Blaskic, who is testifying today as well. Mr. Nobilo, you may begin to exercise your right to redirect after the cross-examination which was conducted by the Prosecutor. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Re-examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yesterday we finished with Prosecutor's Exhibit 38, which is actually Narodni List or, rather, a decree that regulates disciplinary proceedings in the Croatian Defence Council, and now we would like to discuss Article 67. In order to be sure that this is properly translated into all three languages, because I believe this Article to be of key importance for understanding the responsibility of General Blaskic in proceedings, I shall read this, with your permission, very slowly, very clearly, so that every word can be understood. We are going to put the French version on the ELMO. Perhaps it has not been properly translated because obviously my colleague, Mr. Hayman, and I do not know French well enough. After that, I am going to put my questions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the interpreters please receive copies in other languages?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We shall try to give the interpreters the English text at least. So we have the French and the English texts on the ELMO. In addition to that, I'll be reading it out in Croat. So I am reading Article 67 of the disciplinary Rules of Procedure: "The commander of the operative zone - for non-commissioned officers and officers up to the rank of brigadier serving in units or institutions which are subordinate to the operative zone commander --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could we have a very precise translation? You are repeating the word which in French is said "qui en relevent" it says in French. Could we have -- it's important. We have to be very careful about that expression, "qui en relevent." Is it "subordinate" or "falling under the jurisdiction of"? What is the term in Serbo-Croatian that's used? Could you repeat the Serbo-Croatian term, and I'll ask that it be interpreted?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It is about units that are subordinate, "subordinate" in English, to the commander of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So I am reading once again. "The commander of the operative zone - for non-commissioned officers and officers up to the rank of brigadier serving in units or institutions which are subordinate to the operative zone commander, and non-commissioned officers and officers up to the rank of colonel," of brigadier, "serving in administrative agencies and enterprises, and other legal entities within the area under the authority of the operative zone commander."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And the second term "for the administrative organs and the companies and other persons," "se trouvent," "who are," what does that mean, "se trouvent," "who are"? It's not that they are under the authority of or subordinate to but that they are; in French "se trouvent," "are."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, but these are not units, these are institutions, enterprises, and we are going to explain that now. We have two principles, the territorial and the personal. The personal is related to units and the territorial is related to enterprises and institutions. However, now I would like to put a question to General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday that Article was read to you at light speed. Please tell the Court, while you were commander of the Operative Zone, how did you interpret your powers on the basis of Article 67? When I say "powers," I'm talking about disciplinary proceedings.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My interpretation was that I was in charge of units or, rather, officers and non-commissioned officers from units that are directly subordinate to me in the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in this Article, what are the two principles upon which your authority is based?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is based on the principle of subordination, that is to say, subordinate and superior, in respect of units and the territorial principle vis-à-vis institutions, vis-à-vis military enterprises and legal entities. For example, military enterprises, factories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we are going to elaborate the territorial principle, that is to say, those entities over which you have disciplinary authority only because they are within your area. Tell the Court, what could this administration, military administration, be?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It can be the administration for health, the administration for construction, civil engineering, and other administrations that may be in the Operative Zone, or parts of these administrations, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another entity that was subordinate to you, according to the territorial principle, in terms of disciplinary authority, are enterprises. What would that be?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Those would be military enterprises. There were some in that area, military enterprises like, I don't know, the military factory of explosives, of weapons, the depots, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this term, "other legal entities," what would that actually mean? Could you give us an example?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: These could be different military institutes, schooling institutions, military, universities, academies, schools, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All of those were subordinate to you, according to the territorial principle, only because they are in the Operative Zone. And now I'm asking you the following: Which units were subordinate to you and how do you interpret the expression saying that you are in charge of disciplinary proceedings against officers that are in units which are subordinate to the Operative Zone commander?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Units that were within the structure of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia were subordinate to me, and that is how I interpret that principle, that I had authority only over these directly subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in the JNA, where there was the principle of unity of command, when the commander commands all who are within his area, could this kind of a text have existed in the disciplinary rules of the JNA or was it at all?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At any rate, in the JNA, the basic principle was the principle of the unity of command and the unity of responsibility. This was a fundamental principle upon which the disciplinary rules were based, and all military formations that would be in the zone of responsibility of the commander were directly subordinate to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, in respect of translation problems, could we be sure that 52.2 is properly translated, which seems somewhat different to me? Article 52.2 of that same regulation which deals with the problems of the military -- deals with the problems of the military tribunal and uses terms which are somewhat different. Do you see where I am? I want to also show it to my colleagues. I'll show it to Judge Rodrigues here. I would like you to put 52.2 on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Does everybody see where we are? Does the Prosecutor see where we are? 52.2? Mr. Nobilo, could you read that for us, please, and I'll ask the interpreters to be very careful and to look at the text on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: There is an ambiguity here, and we have to be very careful about this. This is the authority of the disciplinary court, the authority of the disciplinary court, Article 52, paragraph 2: "Operative zone military disciplinary courts shall try non-commissioned officers and officers up to the rank of brigadier in units or institutions that are subordinate to the operative zone commander or are in units or institutions within the area under the operative zone commander's authority, as well as non-commissioned officers and officers up to the rank of brigadier serving in the administrative bodies of enterprises and other legal entities." Mr. President, I don't know how the term within the authority --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In French, it says, "ressort," R-E-S-S-O-R-T.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That is the problem. The words "in the area under the authority of" does not necessarily mean territory. It means part of the authority. It is ambiguous. It can refer to territory, but it can also refer to part of the scope of his authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The problem is not one of taking sides. The Judges don't take sides. I'm simply pointing out that in this text, which refers to the command responsibility under the angle of the military tribunal, what is interesting is to see that we have a first level of subordination which is found exactly the same way under 52.2 and 67.2, we have the level of enterprises and other legal entities, like in 67.2, but the precision which is different is that you have the units or establishments in the sector of the operative zone commander. I'm not taking sides. That's not my role. I'm simply here to listen, and I'm asking you only for information about what you're questioning the General on, the General who has a legal specialist with him. I would like to know that when you put those two articles together, didn't it provide enough ambiguity in respect of interpretation that it would not require that the high command would have a very specific definition of his command? It's very important for all of us to be clear on this point, because here, there is a definition which is additional to what is provided in 67.2, and they're not talking about explosive factories or military schools, and they are not speaking about units, and here, I think we agree, that are subordinate. We still have to know what is meant by "subordinate." "Subordinate" means under the orders of. But here there is an addition. There are units within the sector, and that's why I would like you to ask the witness questions about that. I think that Judge Rodrigues also would have a question. Perhaps counsel could answer first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, I would like to ask another question. I would like to know what are the authorities, the competencies of the prosecutor in the military tribunal, and by that, I mean if the prosecutor only issued indictments or if he had authority or jurisdiction over carrying out investigations as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are disciplinary proceedings, and the prosecutor does have the authority to investigate, just as the officer does, but in disciplinary proceedings -- however, before we move further on, I would like to seek the advice of the interpreters, perhaps. It is being said here "the sector of authority." "Sector" implies territory, whereas "area of authority" in Croat does not necessarily imply territory. Because had they thought territory, they would have said "the area" or "the territory" over which the commander has authority. So the word "territory" itself would have been used, the area in which he has responsibility. But here "area," it is realm, it is ambiguous, because the definition is not precise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, I would like to go back to Article 67, and I wish to ask you the following, General: If you are told that you are the superior officer in the Operative Zone to the units that are subordinate to you, does that mean that in the Operative Zone, there are units whose superior officer you are not? How do you interpret that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly, in every operative zone of the HVO, there were units that were not directly subordinate to the commander of the operative zone. So such units did exist, and I did not have authority over such units in military disciplinary proceedings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us disregard the factual situation for a moment, and let us concentrate on Article 67. When you are told -- we're talking about you -- when you, the commander of the Operative Zone, have authority over subordinate units, how do you interpret that in relation to units that are attached to you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Such authority was not given to me over units that were attached, because had the legislator wished to give such authority, then he would, proceeding from the principle of the unity of command which did not exist in the HVO, he would have defined my authority according to territorial principle. However, it is precisely because of the existence of units that were not directly subordinate to the commander, there are these two principles: the principle of subordination and the principle of territorial authority over institutions, enterprises, and legal entities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us be specific. In the sense of Article 67, were the units of the military police and the special purpose unit, Vitezovi, subordinate to you, and were you in charge of military disciplinary proceedings in that respect?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we are going to move on to something else. General, Witness G, on page 3855, mentioned that in Ahmici, in addition to the Jokeri, there were also the Vitezovi and HVO units. What is your knowledge about this? Which units were there? Where were the Vitezovi, to the best of your knowledge, and where were the HVO units?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: According to the report that I received and the reports which I received in the area and sector of Ahmici, the 4th Battalion of the military police was present. The Vitezovi, the Vitezovi unit, had a very precise assignment, to block and protect the hotel from the direction of Stari Vitez and to prevent an attack by the BH army. Part of the units, that is to say, the forces of the Vitez Brigade also had precise assignments, to set up a blockade of the axes of attack by the BH army south of Ahmici, south of the main road running from Vitez to Busovaca, and it did not perform mobilisation, nor did it perform any assignments in the Ahmici sector. Also, from document 250, it can be seen that the Vitezovi arbitrarily performed the action of the attack on the petrol pump, and they took over the Kalen petrol pump later on, in fact. But the unit had a precisely defined assignment, and according to the reports that I received, it was located in front of the hotel, that is to say, between the hotel and Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In document 691, it states that a soldier, who was not a member of the military police, was wounded on the 16th of April somewhere in Santici, that is to say, near Ahmici. What are your comments to that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already stated that the Vitez Brigade had precisely defined assignments south of the road, that is to say, south of Ahmici. Ahmici is to the north of the road, and I believe that it was a question of a non-mobilised soldier of the Vitez Brigade who happened to find himself that morning in the direct vicinity of his house and who was wounded, and confirmation about this wounding he received in order to be able to regulate his invalidity status and other benefits that he would accrue from that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one sentence, please, linked to document 693, 694. In the spring of 1993, did the home guard units, the Domobrani, exist in the Central Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, the home guard units did not exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a corps of command or did you have an assistant for the home guards?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, we were in a stage where we had determined and appointed commanders for the home guard units and in the process of establishing the home guard units, but the war with the BH army, in the spring of 1993, stopped us in this process, and we were not able to implement that project, that is to say, we never actually organised and formed the home guard units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On several occasions in this Tribunal, from various witnesses, an individual named Miroslav Bralo, "Cicko," was mentioned. What do you know about him?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I knew that he was a killer who had committed a crime by killing his next-door neighbour, a Bosniak Muslim, and afterwards he placed an explosive and the body in his house and activated the explosive and blew everything up. He was a pathologically disturbed individual with maniacal characteristics in his behaviour. And I know that after that act and as a decision by the military district court, following a decision by the military district court, he was placed in the military district prison and locked up, he was imprisoned, and at the insistence of myself and the involvement of Ante Sliskovic, the SIS security assistant, he was imprisoned in the military district prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to the best of your knowledge, where was he when the crime in Ahmici took place?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He would have had to have been in the military district prison of Kaonik, imprisoned there, locked up there, in the pre-trial proceedings undertaken by the military district prosecutor, the military district court in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who set him free and what importance does this have? What do you think about that today?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said here in this -- I heard in this Tribunal from the Prosecution witnesses that he was in Ahmici on the 16th of April. I do not know who set him free, but at all events, the individual who is behind his freeing quite certainly is behind what happened in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the time after Ahmici --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Nobilo, for interrupting you. I heard a reference made to the Domobrani. Excuse me for going back to that. But I hadn't seen -- I didn't see the expression in the transcript, I only saw "home guards," but not the words "Domobrani." I would like to be sure that the witness is saying that in the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, there were no Domobrani. I would like to be clear about that issue because I have the idea that at least in the Busovaca region, they were there. So I would like to be sure about that.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did try to establish the Domobran units.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Domobran," the interpretation in English is "home guards."

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: And we had determined the commanders for the home guard units but we never implemented the project, we did not form home guard units in the Operative Zone because the war broke out, the war with the BH army in April '93.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But at least de facto did they exist or did they not exist within your region?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the end of 1994 sometime, we did establish them. There were home guard regiments. But before that, that is to say, in April and in the spring of 1993, we had not established them yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In particular, did they or did they not exist in the Kaonik prison?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the Kaonik prison?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not have data of that kind. As far as I know, they did not exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Rodrigues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Perhaps we could clarify something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Amongst the people, the members of the Busovaca Brigade who were not professionals, did they perhaps call them the Domobrani? So not the official term.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, not only in Busovaca, they called them that everywhere, and it is the local term for soldiers, Croats, and it is a traditional term, the Domobrani, a traditional name.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter notes English translation, "home guards."

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: So that is what they were called. But the military unit of the home guards did not exist up until sometime in 1994. Later on, in Busovaca, there was the home guard regiment. But the people used to call them the Domobrani, particularly the elderly people from 50 to 65 years of age. That was the term generally used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us return to Ahmici. The Prosecutor, on several occasions, said more or less the following, that everybody knew that what had happened -- everybody knew about what had happened in Ahmici except you, and he quoted an example for this. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as Ahmici is concerned, with regard to combat activities between the BH army and the battalion of the military police, I learnt about that on the 16th of April, 1993, at 11.42. However, today, when we talk about Ahmici, they have become a synonym for crime; and at the time, that is, on the 16th, 17th, 18th, and 19th of April, that was not the case. At that time, Ahmici was a synonym for the victory of the members of the HVO over the members of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, was anything known about the crime, on the 17th and 18th?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, and we could see from some evidence put forward by the Prosecutor, I think they were videotapes, although I don't know whether the videotape was ever shown on local television, that it spoke about a military victory of the HVO over the BH army and that not a single word is mentioned about a crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from that television footage, the Prosecutor mentioned several other events or individuals as, by way of an example, of people who knew something about Ahmici and you did not know. How do you view that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mention was made that Mr. Valenta knew about Ahmici. I believe that Mr. Valenta did know about the fighting going on there because what was quoted was two days after Ahmici. I learnt about the fighting in Ahmici two days before Mr. Valenta.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Valenta mention a crime in his quotation?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I never heard at any point that Valenta mentioned a crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A European Monitoring Mission report was mentioned. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that the European Monitors at that time were in the region of Ahmici under the protection of their Warriors, the BritBat, and they arrived at certain knowledge concerning a burnt corpse, a burnt body, and I think several facilities as well, but they did not share that information with me, that is to say, I did not receive information of that kind from them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Reading UNPROFOR's reports, the milinfosum for the 16th of April, 1993, where mention is made of the casualties in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, UNPROFOR had its patrols with its armoured vehicles, known as the Warriors, and their mobile communication devices, and this was deployed in Ahmici, and they sent their operative centre, at their base in Nova Bila, information about the events in Ahmici. However, that information was not sent to me, and to the best of my recollection, Colonel Stewart made a statement for the press and said that he learned about Ahmici after being warned by the soldiers of the BH army and after he had gone to the Ahmici area on the 21st or around the 22nd of April when he sent me the letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Stewart's letter, was that the first news that you received from UNPROFOR related to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That letter was the first news that was concrete news and clear news and informed me that a tragedy had taken place and that a war crime had taken place in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How can you, and can you at all, explain the fact that UNPROFOR, for six days or for five days, hid information about the crime in this way? How can you explain that? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to find an explanation for that action because there was a lot of fighting at about 22 positions, in fact, because they were combat activities in built-up areas. There were a large number of casualties. But I don't know why, on the 16th, they did not share their information with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We heard mention of the Bosniak president of the Muslim wartime presidency of Vitez, that is to say, the highest power and authority of the Bosniaks in Vitez, Dr. Mujezimovic, and his information and knowledge. Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezimovic was the president of the wartime presidency, that is to say, he was the top military and political organ of power and authority in the Vitez area for the Bosniak Muslims, and in a direct conversation with his medical staff, nurses, living in the region of Ahmici, he learnt on the 19th of April about the crime in Ahmici. Therefore, it is obvious that he too learnt about this thanks to the fact that he was in direct communication with the inhabitants of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, on that same day, the 19th of April, the Prosecutor quoted a statement by Dr. Mujezimovic on page 1706 where Cerkez and two or three members of his command mentioned Ahmici. May we have your comments on that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, from that particular comment, we can see that Cerkez was not speaking about the crime in Ahmici but he was speaking about the fighting that had taken place in Ahmici, and I've already said that Ahmici at that time was synonymous with military victory over the BH army and not a synonym of crime as has become the case today or later on when the whole thing was uncovered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you received the first information about some civilian casualties in the Vitez municipality and what were your reactions to that, please?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I received this information, the first information that I received, that is to say, on the 16th of April, 1993, from the representative of the negotiating delegation, Mr. Prskalo and Bilicic, who had returned from negotiations from the UNPROFOR base, at the UNPROFOR base; and already, in the course of the night, sometime around 0400 hours on the 17th of April, issued an order in which I clearly defined and stated that civilians must be protected and that any use of force towards civilians was a crime, and I particularly underlined that and underscored it in my order. I also issued an order on the 18th of April linked to the protection and safety of civilians and also on the 21st of April along with the demand that these orders be acknowledged by signatures of the individual commanders, the commanders of brigades, and that the commanders of the brigades should inform me thereof. I endeavoured to ensure a dual chain so as to be absolutely sure and certain that these orders would be conveyed down the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next information that associated you in your mind to a location around Ahmici was the information you received from Dzemo Merdan on the 20th of April from Zenica. Can you tell us, please, how you understood this information and what you undertook?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was a meeting in Zenica on the 20th of April, 1993, and in a heated atmosphere, when everybody took the floor when they saw fit at the meeting, Dzemo Merdan made his statement, also in a heated fashion, and I suggested that a joint commission be engaged to determine and ascertain the facts with regard to his allegations. When I received this information, I made a note of it, and once I returned to my headquarters, I issued a demand that all reports from the terrain should be collected, and once I was informed that none of the reports went to support that claim and when I became conscious of the fact that the representatives of the BH army, the top representatives at the meeting in Zenica, had immediately passed over that allegation, I then came to understand that it was not a serious allegation but that, quite simply, in a heated discussion of that kind, it was probably something that was stated to improve the negotiating powers of the moment, positions of the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Bob Stewart? When you learned about Ahmici from Bob Stewart and you sent him the emotional letter that you sent him requesting that a joint commission work together, tell us, please, what were your priorities in a situation of that kind? What did you think was the most important thing? The crime had occurred. "Now what shall I do?" What were your thoughts along those lines?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I sent the letter to Bob Stewart requesting a joint commission and also requesting a meeting of the top representatives of the army and the HVO. On the occasion, I did believe that the absolute priority was to ensure a cease-fire, that is to say, to halt the hostilities between the BH army and the HVO and, if possible, to have a separation of forces, to prevent a repetition of the Ahmici crime, and to undertake a full and complete investigation into the crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To prevent a new crime and the speed of an investigation, what would you say came foremost, the way in which you thought at the time?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The absolute priority, of course, was to prevent a fresh evil and a new crime. That was the absolute priority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Prosecutor, on several occasions, asked you, "Why did you not call Pasko Ljubicic in his office and ask him what had happened?" Can you tell us, can you tell the Trial Chamber, if you go back in time to the situation you were in then, why did you not do that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not do that because none of his reports even intimated the crime that had taken place in Ahmici, and I had to protect the investigation into the crime, first and foremost. It was not a disciplinary error or offence which would demand a discussion with him to criticise him or to give him any suggestions. What we had before us was a very serious and grievous crime, and everything had to be done to protect the investigation into that crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you understand, methodologically speaking, this matter? When do you talk to a suspect, at the beginning of an investigation or at the end of an investigation? What do you think about police or investigative methodology?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I never attended courses on the subject, and I am not professionally trained to conduct an investigation, but I considered it necessary, first of all, to collect facts and evidence, and only then, once that had been done, to confront the suspects with this evidence and these facts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you not undertake an investigation yourself? Why did you not interview people and investigate generally? Why?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: First of all, I endeavoured, as commander of the Operative Zone, the position I held, to work within the system. I was not a professional nor was I trained during my years of schooling in matters of investigation and conducting investigations, and I considered that it was my duty to ensure that the system functioned properly, and that means that the investigation be conducted by the competent authorities and by the trained and professional authorities in that sphere, and that was the security service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, from the time the crime in Ahmici occurred on the 16th up until the beginning of the investigation, somewhere around the 24th, eight days had elapsed. Do you consider that this passage of time, some eight, ten, fifteen days, had any vital effect or could have had a vital effect on the quality of the investigation? How do you view that problem, the problem of the passage of time?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I personally think that that problem of the passage of time did not have any significant reflection on the quality of the investigation, particularly if we keep in mind the situation that we were in at the time. First of all, data was collected about the corpses, and there was a medical investigation with a description of the causes of death. The homes that were burned more or less remained in that area, and I think that the most important part of the investigation was to collect personal evidence, i.e., to carry out interviews with the suspects and to find out who commanded, planned, and committed the crime. These were the most important questions, as far as I understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you choose SIS, the Security and Information Service, to conduct an investigation on Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: By law, its authority was the only authorised body to conduct an investigation of the members of the military police. So it was the only service that had such authority and that had the expertise and the capability to conduct such an investigation. I could not request the military police to conduct an investigation of itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated that your absolute priority after Ahmici was to prevent a new crime from taking place. We won't be producing any documents, but can you remember what you did in the days of the 22nd of April and on, after you found out about the crime in Ahmici from Colonel Stewart?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I issued a series of orders which I tried to implement on the ground, and I will cite just a number of those orders. These are Defence Exhibits 318, 334, 336, 338, 353, 361, 362, 364, 365, 366, 370, 374, and 376. I also said at a press conference, I condemned the crime, and I think that this had an exceptional influence on public opinion, all the more so because that condemnation of mine reached each home and each family in the Lasva pocket through the local media. I also asked representatives of international humanitarian organisations, representatives of the Red Cross, the UNHCR, to clarify their mandate and to address, through the local television, the people and the refugees who were living in that area so that they could also have an effect, at least to alleviate the hatred that was present amongst the refugees which made the situation more difficult and more complex. Personally, also at meetings with commanders of the brigades, I checked and tried to make sure that each order reached each soldier on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We talked a lot about document 456/58, and this is the order that you sent to Colonel Stewart at the general staff and to the head of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. We will not look at this document, but could you just please define what this document represents? How do you define it? What is that supposed to represent?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The document is called "Information about the meeting with Colonel Bob Stewart," and I would dispatch information about meetings to my superiors, as well as this information, and I would usually state what I got from the participants at the meeting, what I stated, and a proposal for certain measures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell us whether that document represents a report on the crime in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, not in any case does that document represent that. It's exclusively information about the meeting with Colonel Stewart. All reports of my activities regarding the investigation and everything that is connected to Ahmici, I would usually -- I would always send that along.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you interpret that this information was sent by regular fax to Mostar and not by packet link, which was the usual manner of communication, and it was protected in a way, as we heard yesterday?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In that information about the meeting, of course, the third party, Bob Stewart himself who participated in the meeting, was informed. There was nothing in the contents of the meeting that needed to be protected, and for documents that were not orders or did not contain operative information, I tried to send those documents by fax because the communications were quite burdened, and I believed that there was no need for such protection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of this trial, a question kept coming up, at least I felt it that way, and we could formulate it in the following way: Bob Stewart and other representatives of the international organisations, why did you not inform them about your information about Ahmici, which unit committed it, the chain of command of the unit, the persons who were possibly responsible, in accordance with that chain of command, who would have issued the orders, and also about your problems with the military police? Why did you not at that time, in April or May of '93, not present that to the International Community? Maybe your fate would have been different.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My fate may have been different in that case; however, there were legal regulations which I respected. They are about military secrets. I never talked about weaknesses within the HVO, the problems with dual command and unified responsibility and other weaknesses, I never shared those problems with international representatives because I was aware myself that both they, as well as their interpreters to a certain extent, would convey such information later to the other side, to the enemy, to the BH army or the HVO. On the other hand, I did not have authorisation, after I realised that international institutions did not participate in the investigation, that I could not share such information with unauthorised persons. I did not convey these weaknesses and all of these problems to them because I would thereby be violating the military secret regulations. Also, it would have made it more difficult regarding survival because the BH army would find out all about our internal weaknesses, and this could then come to the fore when they were carrying out their attacks in their attempts to take over that territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Contrary to the regulations on military secrets and contrary to the orders that you had, this, that you have now -- if you had said to the representatives of the International Community what you have just told this Court, who were not members of the HVO, what would have happened to you? What would this have meant?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I would have violated internal rules of the HVO. That was for sure. But it is difficult to forecast what it would have meant further because probably the consequences of it all would have been different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court how you conducted yourself in front of international factors and the B and H army? What was the HVO picture that you presented to them; could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: From the first meeting in Sarajevo, the tripartite meeting where U.N. representatives were present and also representatives of the UNHCR and other international institutions, together with representatives of the B and H army and representatives at that time of the army of Republika Srpska, at that time everybody who took the floor took the floor in an attempt to protect all internal weaknesses and concealing, to a certain degree, all the problems that were present among the ranks of the army and the HVO regarding structure. This was an army, an armed peoples -- an army that just needed to be organised and structured. But regardless of that, fighting and combat activities needed to be conducted. But in any case, this was a monolithic-structured military formation, and in that way, we wanted to leave the impression in front of the others and also taking upon ourselves a little bit the responsibility regarding the implementation of our responsibilities despite all of the internal problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judge Rodrigues, at one moment, asked you, Why did you not resign? Your officers lied to you, they committed a crime behind your back, and yet you are sitting here because of that today. Were they worth such a sacrifice? That was the question of Judge Rodrigues. Today, now that you think about it, what would your answer be?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Perhaps those who lied to me, I'm sure that they are not worth my sacrifice. However, the people who lived there and who fought for their survival, their biological survival, they were worth my sacrifice. And in spite of everything, I stated then also that I wanted to stay with those people; and, in spite of everything, achieve my three priorities, meaning: survival, prevention from a crime happening again, and carrying out the investigation. I don't believe that any captain of a sinking ship would leave that ship first and abandon it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you had resigned, what would have happened? Who would have been the commander? How would events have proceeded? Do you have any idea about that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The radio, the media, under the authority of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, published at one moment that a new commander of the Operative Zone was Zarko Andric and his deputy was Darko Kraljevic. I believe that events would have become even more radical and that perhaps there would have been much more, much greater chaos, and perhaps Ahmici would have happened again and perhaps members of the B and H army, if they had entered Busovaca and Vitez, would have committed even greater crimes since it was very difficult to control their hatred, just as it was in their entry in Buhine Kuce, Krizancevo Selo, and other areas that the HVO was losing and then managing to take back. Perhaps there would have been even more massacres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On several occasions -- Mr. President, should we stop now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to ask General Blaskic whether you still maintain that 456/58 is incomplete?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It's not a document that I wrote and that I sent; it's incomplete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I was a little surprised because you said so often during the cross-examination that you didn't remember today, that the essential part of that document did not really express what you really thought, and I was wondering whether you had changed your argument in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I did not ask him that. The sense of my question was: What was the nature of the document? A report from a meeting. We spoke a lot about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo -- but I remember it so clearly, when there was that very long conversation about 456/58, that everything would have been different if we had been able to see in that document all of the nuances that had been introduced into it. Remember in 456/58, you remember your client even said to us that it seemed ridiculous to him, the document seemed ridiculous, because it seemed that it was putting into Colonel Stewart's mouth words about the meeting with Mate Boban whereas, in fact, the dash was missing which would remind us that the General, et cetera. So I was surprised that today your client didn't remember the discussion about that document, and I want to be sure that you still claim what you said before, that is, that the document is incomplete. I suggest that we take a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. Please be seated. Mr. Nobilo, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, what about your closest associates? Who were the persons and what posts were involved?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was the chief of staff, who was my deputy at the same time, that is to say, that he held two posts, and he was in charge of all operative staff activities and practically all combat documents that he elaborated and then made proposals of various solutions. Then there were the assistants for personnel affairs, the assistants for organisation, mobilisation and the establishment, then the assistant for logistics, for the security service, for information and propaganda activity, and other assistants. These are a commander's closest associates that comprise that body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this trial, the Defence presented as evidence your order dated the 10th of May, 1992, concerning the investigation of the crime in Ahmici. You said that you gave an oral order to the assistant for SIS earlier, on the 24th of April, 1993. My learned colleague, the Prosecutor, asked you at one point, "Do you have any proof except for your own word that you issued this earlier order orally concerning Ahmici?" What do you say to this Honourable Court?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The very fact that a member of one's immediate staff is given an order in writing is telling proof of an exception, that something had to happen before that that I was not fully satisfied with and that this was additional pressure that was brought to bear against my immediate associate so that the assignment that was given earlier could be carried out fully; that is to say, that this body works in a team-like fashion, these are my closest associates, and during the day, we usually have one or -- several briefings and then assignments are issued orally, but they are registered in an official document which was called the personal war diary of each and every officer. I had such a personal war diary myself as well as all my associates. Every task would be registered, written down there, and then it would be commented upon very briefly at these briefings. I am claiming before this Court that I do not recall having ever issued an order in writing to my deputy, who was also chief of my staff, or any other associates. This was truly very rare and an exception, that to give this closest team of closest associates orders in writing except in these exceptional situations that I already mentioned which were telling proof in their own right that I was not fully satisfied with the action that I ordered previously. The very fact that the order in writing was issued on the 10th of May showed that something had happened earlier between me and the security assistant, something that I was not pleased with, and that this was additional pressure on him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to this being additional pressure on him, what does it mean when you give your assistant, whom you sit with together at the same table every day and who works with you in team-like fashion, when you give him a written order? What does that mean for your personal relationship and what does that mean in an official sense too?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as personal relations, it certainly means that this is a statement of mistrust or dissatisfaction with the extent to which a previous assignment had been carried out, but it is also a warning to a commander or an assistant to whom such an order was given that he should bear in mind that he has to carry out that assignment and that otherwise this order, like previous orders, would be additional material proof if such an associate is held accountable or is made to answer for his actions. So this is an additional warning or additional pressure that one cannot just give up on one's assignments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Was there a verbal order given to General Marin; is that what you mean? Is that what you're saying, Colonel Blaskic? To which associate? You said -- I don't remember. I don't remember. I just want to refresh my memory. Did you give it to General Marin? I'm talking about the order.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: General Marin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [interpretation cuts in] ... what General Marin said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, this -- no, no, no. No. This is an order issued orally to the SIS assistant for the investigation in Ahmici, and the witness is trying to say that he gave an oral order before the written order. Proof that an oral order was given is the fact that he gave a written order because he would never do that to his own assistants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. I couldn't remember to whom the verbal order had been given. Yes, it was Mr. Slisovsky, something like that, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Sliskovic, yes. Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I also don't remember, General Blaskic, when General Marin came, did he confirm your verbal order -- well, we can find it in the transcript -- but did he confirm the order or not, or don't you remember? Judge Rodrigues says he didn't confirm it.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: General Marin is not a member of this team within the command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I thought he was your deputy. I thought he was your deputy. Not at that time?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, no. He was never my deputy, Your Honour. He was subordinate to the chief of staff, that is to say, he is three levels below me. He is subordinate to the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But he participated in the meetings, didn't he, when the verbal orders were given? He was at the meetings every day, was he not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not at my meetings. He is not a member of my team, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: He was the commander of the operations, he was the chief of staff of the operations in the midst of the war. Didn't he come to your meetings every morning? I don't understand. He came for six weeks and he said that he would participate in meetings every morning. Well, what meetings was he participating in?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll try to do this in the right order. First of all, he took part in meetings when the chief of staff was not present, that is to say, when the chief of staff was absent, then ex officio the chief of operations replaces him. But my deputy was always the chief of staff, Mr. Franjo Nakic, and he was always present at the meeting of this team within the command, and only when Nakic would not be there, then Mr. Slavko Marin would come in as Nakic's deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: However, in the midst of the war, did Mr. Marin come to the meetings in order to speak about war operations? You're saying he never came? He was downstairs with the map and he would never come upstairs to see you? You have to admit that that's very surprising.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Marin is a member of the staff. I can show this very easily. I can draw a diagram for you and I can show you his exact position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, that isn't necessary. We'll find it all in the transcript. I don't want to take up Defence time. I was just a little bit surprised. But it's not important. It was just a clarification. I wanted to refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am going to use my own questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please let the General answer. I'm asking him a question.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, only in a situation when the chief of staff was not there, when he was present, it is only then that his deputy comes to attend the meetings of this team within the command, that is, Slavko Marin. There were such situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Okay, I understand.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As to regular situations, regular situations, when the chief of staff is in headquarters, he is a member of this team of mine, and Slavko Marin is his subordinate. He does not take part in the meetings of my team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. I was trying to help you, General, because basically you're looking for proof of the verbal order, which you can't demonstrate because it was a verbal order, and that's true, that's difficult for you. I was saying to myself that if Ahmici was a war operation, which is what you said to us a little while ago, Ahmici was a combat operation, since you even said Anto Valenta said that there was a victory, Ahmici was a victory, so it was part of combat. For you, it was not a crime. First of all, it was a place where combat took place. Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was synonymous at that time, they thought that these were combat operations between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. So I was moving ahead to see if you couldn't somehow improve the existence of the verbal order in a different way, and I was saying to myself that since we were talking about combat operations, around Colonel Blaskic, they must have spoke about combat every day. I would assume that one speaks about combat in the midst of a war. At your staff meetings, you would talk about combat, I assume. No?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In headquarters, everything that was said in the operative centre was registered in the operations logbook, that is to say, every activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But you can't show us the logbook. I would have been very happy for you to present it to us. Unfortunately, you never found your own log. Let me remind you that you never found it, not even when you were involved with the Operation Spider. You didn't find the log, and I was very sorry that you didn't. It seemed to me that all chiefs in a war would preserve traces of their own diaries or logs. You know, this is something which happens in every country. All chiefs have traces of what they did. But I put myself in your place, and I say that this verbal order, which is a very important one for you, on the 20th of April or the 21st of April, you gave a verbal order, and I was saying that, after all, in the meetings where there were many members of the staff and you were involved in speaking about the combats, didn't you speak about the fighting in Ahmici, and didn't somebody say, "Oh, yes, the fighting in Ahmici, it didn't go well. There were people killed. There were crimes," et cetera. It must have happened that way.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, not that way. I got a letter from Colonel Stewart about what had happened in Ahmici, and after the letter, I had a meeting with Colonel Stewart, and I reacted by issuing an order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General Blaskic, I was trying to reason along with you, but I think that this diary is lost, and we only have your word as a soldier and your word as a sworn statement. I think that's all we can say for now. I'm not asking any further questions. I was just thinking that in a general staff meeting with General Marin, who was involved with the operations, you were in the middle of war, Ahmici was being spoken about, you spoke about it as being a victory, if this has a connection, a consistency, and I was saying perhaps by looking through all of these elements, General Blaskic would be able to show us the probability of the existence of that verbal order. No, you can't, and you're simple saying, "I gave a verbal order and, believe me, it's true." The Judges will see what they have to do. Mr. Hayman is also going to help you, and Judge Rodrigues also has a question he'd like to ask. I'm not going to ask any further questions. I think that you don't have any, General, and that's that. Be careful of your microphone, Mr. Hayman. Mr. Hayman, did you want to make a comment? Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We do, of course, disagree with some of your comments, Mr. President, that the only evidence is his word that there was no order, and we have some follow-up questions that I've asked Mr. Nobilo to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You're right. You're absolutely right. But Judge Rodrigues also has questions. I agree with you -- I know that you wouldn't be in agreement with what I said, but it's my right to ask the General whether, instead of repeating, as he has been repeating when he said I gave a verbal order, whether there wasn't a way through other channels in order to corroborate. I am in a system, Mr. Hayman, in which one does not have written proof, one tries to corroborate. That's all I'm trying to say. For the time being, I have some trouble in following this, and I'm trying to reason the way your client is reasoning to see whether, through another approach, through the meetings of the general staff, one could have some type of real probability of the existence of the verbal order. That's all I'm saying, and it's my right to ask that question. That's what I was saying. I think that Mr. Nobilo wants to say something. Yet first I'd like Judge Rodrigues to ask his question, and then we can give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, we have proof, but you just have to give us the floor. We have an explanation. We have a different method.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'll give the floor to Judge Rodrigues. I'm not going to take the floor away from Judge Rodrigues, but I saw Mr. Hayman with such ardour and conviction saying that -- reacting to my questions, I have to respond to that, and this is your time. We're not going to take it away from you. I'll give the floor to Judge Rodrigues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I'll ask this question very quickly so as not to take away Defence time. Here is my question, General. More or less, approximately, how many general meetings took place between the 16th of April and the 22nd of April, more or less?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Until the 22nd of April, every day, we were sitting in one room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Therefore, every day, even on Saturdays and Sundays?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: My second question: There were at least five meetings. At any meeting, did you speak about the victory in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Rodrigues. I didn't express myself well, but that's what I was trying to get at. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: At some point in some meeting, did you speak about the victory in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I only requested, when I arrived from Zenica, I think this was around the 20th of April, late at night, to have all the reports on combat operations submitted to me in Ahmici, Nadioci, Sivrino Selo, all these places along the road. I never -- I personally, if you're asking me -- I never thought this was a victory, because basically we were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. You said that for the HVO it was a victory. Today, Ahmici means crime, but at that time, it meant victory. Therefore, I can ask you the question in another way: At any of the meetings that you had together, did you speak about the fighting in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: About the fighting according to the reports that I had received, the BH army and the military police, yes. About combat, combat was mentioned, combat operations, positions that were taken, things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: And while speaking about the combat, even in respect of the military police with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did somebody speak about the fighting, that is, how that could be translated as being a victory, that is, how the fighting occurred and what the consequences were?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In that period of time, these were still situations while the fighting was ongoing, so the discussions were based on the reports that we had received, on the basis of the information I received about momentary positions, about combat operations with the army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But, General, I'm speaking especially about Ahmici. Did you speak or did somebody speak about the fighting which had taken place in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Specifically, at that point in time, I personally did not speak about this. I asked for the report to be checked out, and when they told me that the reports were about momentary positions and there was nothing unusual as compared to things that were happening at some 20 places or so, there were no other discussions in that point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I have to ask you another question. I believe that I know there were about five or six people at that meeting. How many people participated at that daily meeting, team meeting?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At different times, well, it differed, five to six and depending on the subject matter that was to be discussed, and there were people who had various engagements. At first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: General, it was five to six. I understand that on one day there might be a meeting with four people and another day there would be six people. But between the 16th of April and the 22nd of April, nobody present at the meeting spoke about the fighting in Ahmici, or did somebody, in fact, speak about it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that time, the fighting was still ongoing, and we received reports and we reacted to the reports that we received. This can be seen from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. I think you understand my question. I'm speaking about the reports and the information in respect of Ahmici. I'm not speaking about others. I'm speaking about Ahmici, specifically about Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about the same, Your Honour, Ahmici, that fighting was taking place there, that units of the BH army were fortified, I remember around the school and around the mosque, and that there was combat going on over there, that the front line was being suppressed and that the BH army is moving to their reserve positions about 50 metres above the village, that there were combat operations going on over there too, so there was such information coming in, that is to say, such military reports. Yes, I did receive them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: And the information for you and for those people who were present at the meeting, was the information positive or negative?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The information spoke of how heavy the fighting was, and I think they were sort of half/half. The front was moving towards the north, it went to the north of the village, but at least from a tactical point of view, it had not reached such a level --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: General, if somebody spoke about violent activity, perhaps that person spoke about the violence in the sense of winning or losing a battle, do you have any idea about this violence which would entail a positive or a negative attitude? I'm talking about the HVO side, positive or negative reactions from the HVO side?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the fighting went on practically all day between HVO units and BH army units, and the fighting was rather static, operations were rather static, and only in the coming period did the front line move a bit. Even at a tactical level, this was negligible. So this negligible movement was to the detriment of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina but that was only temporary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me. When you say that the fighting went on all day, what day are you speaking about?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm speaking about the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: And the fighting was taking place on that day in Ahmici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: According to the information I had, sometime between 11.45, when I received it, in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me, General, for insisting on this point, but I would like you to answer my questions directly. When somebody spoke about the fighting which was going on with a great deal of violence on the 16th of April in Ahmici, did the idea of violence bring out a negative or a positive attitude on the side of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: According to the reports and according to my memory --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me. My question is, the idea of violence that somebody mentioned at the meeting, and you said that there was violent combat going on, my question is, and the answer, in my opinion, should either be "Yes," "No," or "I don't know." This is the question: The idea of violence entailed a positive idea or a negative reaction, that is, a reaction of success or failure in respect of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'll try to give you the most accurate answer possible, Your Honour. I believe, according to those reports, and as far as I can remember now, that this fighting was one on a footing of equality --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: According to what was said at the meeting, not according to the reports, but according to what was said at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, according to what was said at the meeting, this was static fighting that was ongoing, without any movement of the front line. This went on on both sides, static fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Your Honour, the interpretation is the problem. General Blaskic uses the word "silina" which is being interpreted into English as "violence." These are two different words. They have a different meaning. We are talking about the intensity of fighting, and violence is something different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In any case, according to what you say, I'll change the way I express myself. Instead of using the word "violence," I'll use the word "intensity." So, General, when somebody at the meeting spoke about the fact that the fighting was intense, was fierce, was there the possibility of concluding or did somebody actually say or express a positive or negative idea from the point of view of the HVO? So when I say "positive," "negative," what I mean by those words, I'm connecting them with success or probability of success for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On that day, the 16th, when we're talking about the 16th, this was static combat. There were no movements, and there were no successes. I'm talking about both sides. The two sides were confronting one another and they were firing at one another on the 16th. The next day, there was some movement, perhaps 100 or 150 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: The next morning at what time?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If you allow me to have a look at my chronology? I mean, we're talking about minutes, Your Honour. I don't know. I can't say just off the cuff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Was it 8.00? Was it 11.00? Was it 5.00 in the morning? What time? At what time were you speaking that way?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'll have a look in my chronology and I'll tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I don't think that's necessary. You simply have to say at 9.00, 10.00, 11.00. You have no idea?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it's hard for me to engage in guesswork. We are talking about 22 different places where there was combat activity going on, and from one minute to another, these actions were taking place all over, and I can look at my chronology and tell you very precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So as not to take up too much of the Defence time, perhaps you could look at that during the break. I think that for right now, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Rodrigues. I would like the Defence to understand, and I insist on that, that for the Judges, these are very important moments in respect of the charges and all of us are looking for the truth. This means if, at some time on the 22nd of April, for the first time Colonel Stewart informed your client of the atrocities which had taken place on the -- that's on the 22nd of April, informed him of the atrocities and said, as early as the 22nd of April, you were given verbal orders which apparently were corroborated by the written order of 10 May -- that's the interpretation -- it is true that the Judges are seeking, in all of your client's words, a way to find corroboration for that since there is no formal proof. But we all know that in all legal systems, formal proof, of course, is the best. But it is not absolutely necessary. In all legal systems, people know that the Judges come to decisions in relation to written proof but also through all types of other considerations. It was simply this search for the truth that we have been entrusted with finding. Thank you, Judge Rodrigues, for trying to contribute something. Judge Shahabuddeen, do you wish to say something? Thank you. Mr. Nobilo, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. After a question about Ahmici, I will go back to the substance, and that is to say, that there is other evidence apart from the written type that the order had been given for an investigation into Ahmici previously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I'm going to ask you this now: In the army, among the people, Ahmici was considered to be a victory. You, as a strategist, what do you consider, staying in the village for one day, did this prove advantageous to the HVO or not and where should the HV have been for that one day? So was it a victory or not a victory?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It, of course, was not a victory. I said that the people understood it in this way, the layman spoke about it in that fashion, but on a tactical level, a trained professional commander of a platoon even wouldn't have assessed this as a victory, a trained soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, when you led the operation -- had you led the operation in the village of Ahmici, what would you have done on that day, the 16th of April? What would your manoeuvre have been?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At all times, the principle is to manoeuvre, that is, to avoid combat activities in a built-up area at all costs, and there is no commander whatever who would agree to planning an operation and forget the fact that it would be fighting in the centre of a village. Perhaps Grbavica is the best example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Our time is running out, so I am beginning to think like my colleague, Mr. Kehoe, so let's stop there. Could you explain to the Judges what you mean by "manoeuvre"? Where should you have gone and arrived at had you led the operation?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The hill above the village and taken it from the left and right, that is to say, quite certainly to avoid any fighting in the village. That is the tactic that professional soldiers apply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After 11.42, when you had learnt about fighting in Ahmici, what did you ask Pasko Ljubicic, who led the operation, to do?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On several occasions, once again, I said "Go to the hills. Take to the hills. On the left and flank, go up and take the hills." And that was a similar situation in Gomionica, Grbavica, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us return to the order about Ahmici. Tell us, please, once again, was Slavko Marin a member of your team?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, in the days of the war, the first days of the war, the 16th of April, the 17th of April, the 18th of April, was Nakic at the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Marin replace Nakic on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did Nakic turn up for the first time?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think it was on the 20th of April, and I'm quite certain that it was on the 21st of April. It might have been 20th but certainly the 21st.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After Nakic, the chief of staff of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, succeeded in turning up at the command, did Slavko Marin attend the meetings of your team?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, he never attended the meetings of the team when Franjo Nakic was in the headquarters. So Slavko Marin never attended meetings of my team at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A demand for a request into the investigation into Ahmici and for punishment, is that part of combat operations? Does that come under Slavko Marin's field of activity or not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us once again, please, in concise terms, why do you consider that the fact of issuing a written order to your assistant for investigation into Ahmici was, at the same time, proof that before a written order was issued, an oral order was issued? Why do you consider that that is proof in itself?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
