utterances.text: Because all the commands of all armies, as far as I know, work as a team, they have teamwork and a team approach to their work and function in similar ways, that is to say, they issue oral orders which are then recorded in personal war diaries, and the fact that a written order is issued shows that the superior commanding officer is not satisfied with the results so far or wishes to accelerate those results.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you enumerate for us and tell us, when you give a written order to a member of your own team, what drastic cases are these when that is done?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They are cases when a trust has been upset, the balance of trust, or cases when something truly dramatic occurs between the commander and his immediate assistant, direct assistant, but these are exceptionally rare, very rare cases indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If somebody refuses to carry out an order, would that be a case in point?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Not only refusal but obstruction. You don't have to refuse to carry out an order; you can receive an order and then tell your superiors that this has not been done fully, accomplished fully, so it can be that an order is obstructed in being carried out but threats and warnings to your subordinates that they must implement the order issued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If a written order is a threat and warning, what do you think? Is it, militarily speaking, logical that somebody who you have asked for the first time to carry out an investigation, to send out threats and cautions?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That practically never happens at the level of the brigade or the team of the brigade commander. What always happens is that oral orders are issued to the team, the immediate team, and personal wartime diaries are, of course, official documents as well, and then only if something dramatic takes place or if a commander expresses a certain amount of distrust, only then is a written order issued, but that is truly the exception.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, you have described the order for an investigation of the 10th of May, 1993 as an exception, but you issued another order, once again in writing. Could you tell us what happened in that continuity? Have you noted down how many times and when you asked for, called for an investigation into Ahmici, if you have those notes at hand? If not, we can look into it during the break. But tell us, why did you give a second order in writing as well?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The first report was fairly superficial, and the investigation and the first report did not bring in any concrete results, but it's stated that the investigation would continue. I continued to insist on several occasions -- and in my chronology, I had that -- when I asked for the additional results of the investigation to be sent in to me, and I wanted to create a better climate for the investigation itself, which meant to break down the command structure of the military police and to take over via the commander, Palavra, the military police and a complete change of cadres in the military police, that is, to remove those with criminal records and to create a better security and safety situation for the implementation of a comprehensive investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now move on to something else related to Ahmici. Tell us, please, whether the assistant for security, Ante Sliskovic, was under your exclusive orders and control?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, he was directly subordinate to the chief of the Mostar administration for security, and the orders that he received directly from his superiors had absolute priority compared to my own orders and demands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General Blaskic, in the order of the 10th of May, what's the "ONO"? I see "ONO," chief of operations and training, "ONO." Could we give the document to the General, please? I've got the document in French. Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have it, Mr. President, and it is the operations and training organ of the military district of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is that Mr. Marin?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. He was the head of the operations and training department or office of the military district of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Therefore, I deduce that in the order of 10 May, further to what -- I called him General, but I made a mistake, I mean Judge Rodrigues -- further to what Judge Rodrigues said to you, at some point a relationship was made in your mind between the atrocities, the crime that was committed in Ahmici, and the combat operation in Ahmici. There must have been a connection, and I assume you made that connection. Perhaps you don't understand my question. Let me repeat it. My concern is always to learn how we can corroborate the verbal order. You're saying that "I gave a written order and that it was exceptional which proves a contrario that I gave the order." Therefore, I had the order of 10 May given to me by the registrar, and in the order, you designate, as the person responsible for the investigation, the SIS, the S-I-S, and you say that the SIS took its orders in Mostar. That's possible. Nonetheless, you are the one who was in charge of the investigation; do you agree? You were in charge of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, I requested an investigation of the assistant for security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, no, no, not at all. I've already pointed out to you already during the cross-examination that the number 1 point in the order was to gather all information. When it says "gather information and submit a report about the events," that is a way of conducting an investigation, of considering that one is responsible for an investigation. If what you said is true and if it was consistent with what you've been saying, you would have only issued order 2, "that I appoint the assistant to be responsible for that task." But your assistant is responsible for executing your order under point 1. I'm also speaking for your Defence counsel. But that is not my question. I wanted to ask, but I don't want to use up the Defence's time. We can consider that you yourself took responsibility for the operation. But that doesn't matter. That is not my question. My question is further to comments by Judge Rodrigues. You are obliged, when you designate the assistant at the SIS, the security service, you have to make the connection with Marin who was the chief of operations. You had to have been, "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was customary that all documents were also sent to the operative section, so all the documents I have here I'm sure they do in the operative section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm not talking about what is habitual. I'm speaking about this particular document. When you designate a service which has nothing to do with Ahmici, that is, the security service, you remember you did not want to designate the military police commander for the investigation because you considered that they would not carry out the investigation objectively. I accept that. And so you designate a service which knows nothing about the fighting in Ahmici. They don't know anything about the fighting in Ahmici; you agree with that. In fact, you chose them for that reason, so that they would be objective. Do you follow what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were the professional service for conducting investigations over all institutions, including myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Well, don't answer me in theoretical terms. Please answer precisely. You chose them because they were not the military police, about whom you had suspicions. So they knew nothing about the fighting in Ahmici. Nothing. They were not competent.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not getting any interpretation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think perhaps there was an interpreter problem here. I'm speaking slowly on purpose so they can be very careful that everything I say is interpreted correctly. You designate the assistant from SIS because, in your eyes, he matches the conditions necessary for complete objectivity; is that true or is it not true?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, complete objectivity. Above them is only the joint commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: They did not know what had happened in Ahmici at the point that you designated them. They didn't know.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what information they had at their disposal. The security service is in charge of internal security, but I do believe that they did not know all the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But they did not have jurisdiction over combat matters; that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They did not have jurisdiction over combat, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, that's clear. Therefore, in my opinion, you were obliged to tell them to contact the people or the person responsible for the operations, that's Marin, "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I consider that I was not duty-bound to tell them that, Your Honour. They have power and authority to exert control over everything --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But you did. You designated them as addressees in the order; that is, you considered that there was a relationship that should be made between the two. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They are independent in conducting investigations. They are professional individuals and independent and autonomous in conducting investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure that [interpretation cuts out] ... but if you want to share your conviction with us and you have a very strong conviction, when you say that you wanted to ascertain the truth, when you designated SIS, you had to say to them in some way, "Get information about what happened in that well-known victory in Ahmici, at the intense and fierce combat in Ahmici." That's what you said to Judge Rodrigues. You had to make the connection, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Perhaps I don't understand the question properly, Mr. President, but my knowledge is that SIS --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Okay. I'll repeat it. You ask an investigative service, which is independent, to gather evidence about what you know on the 10th of May about Ahmici, but you know that there had been atrocities that you learned about in Colonel Stewart's letter. You said that you gave verbal orders between the 20th of April and the 10th of May. My question has to do with the written order of 10 May. I would like to know whether you made a connection between General Marin, the chief of your operations, and the assistant at SIS, "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I personally did not connect him because I thought that the assistant for SIS has the authority to have insight into all documents, not only operative ones, but all documents related to the military district.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Your own document is contradicting you because you made that connection, it's indicated in the addressees -- just a moment, please, Mr. Nobilo. You're talking about the operation officers and you said that it was Marin.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, because all the documents go to the operative department, all documents issued go to the operative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. All the documents are transmitted. Therefore, my question, which I'm asking in order to corroborate the verbal order which you allegedly issued, in the team meetings that you had, at some point did you say to Marin, "Marin, I'm going to entrust SIS with the investigation. You're going to be questioned by them in order to find out what happened in Ahmici." Did you do that or did you not do that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not do that because Marin was never a member of my team. Should that have been done, it would have been done by the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are the officer in that headquarters. There's a war, it was an atrocious war, and you're answering in terms of an organisational structure. What I'm trying to find out is a way of corroborating your moral concern about the atrocities in Ahmici. I'm trying to find out whether, in accordance with your order of 10 May, you said at some point to Marin, in fact, "Make available to yourself SIS in order to find out everything you can about Ahmici." Did you do that or didn't you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The file regarding Ahmici was made with the chief of staff on the 22nd, I think, of April. Everything that existed was at their disposal, and I was at the disposal of SIS. So SIS had the power and authority, independent of my own will, to conduct investigations over the whole of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, we'll reread the entire transcript of General Marin. I want to know whether, at some point, you said to Marin, in fact, "Do you remember that on the 20th of April I gave an order in order to find out what happened about the crime in Ahmici? I'm going to repeat the order of 10 May. You're one of the addressees. Did you give all the information about the combat in Ahmici, that is, military activity in Ahmici?"

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not have any discussion with Slavko Marin about that in particular but I did with Franjo Nakic, the chief of staff, and this was about the 22nd of April. I had a meeting with Franjo Nakic, I compiled the file of all reports, and that file was at the disposal of the security service. So all the operations reports and orders from the 15th, 16th, up until the 22nd of April. That was a file containing about 80 to 100 documents placed at the disposal of the security service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Then the file was pretty well done, it was compiled properly. Therefore, my last question is, why re-issue an order on the 10th of May? You've got 180 (sic) documents which unfortunately disappeared. So work was done. Now you're saying that in the order of 10 May, gather or collect all information for several days. There's been rumours in the public -- well, these were not rumours because you're telling me that on the 25th of April, you had a file with 80 or 100 documents in it about the atrocities in Ahmici. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, that was a file about all the operations, all the reports, all the orders, not a file on the crime in Ahmici on the 22nd of April, 1993. The rumours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [interpretation cuts in] ... file on Ahmici. All right. I have no further questions. Judge Rodrigues?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Very quickly, General. Is there a difference between the addressee in your oral order and the addressee in your written order?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I issue an oral order, the recipient must write it down in his personal log, in his official document. I also have it written down in my logbook. If I issue a written order, then it must go to the addressee. A copy also should go to the archives, and one copy should go to the operations and training centre which then distributes all of these documents, and then one of the officers of that department will monitor the implementation of all the issued orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Therefore, General, the conclusion must be that your assistant for security knew what it was about when he received the written order.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he knew that if he was given a written order, that I was not satisfied with the result of the oral order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: And General Marin?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is not an order to act for Brigadier Marin. He receives this order, gives it to his assistant of operations, and then he would classify this document, saying that it was issued on that date, and then he would set it aside for the security service to act upon it. So he only needs to enter it into the logbook to note that it has been issued. He does not act upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was a General or a Brigadier, but Slavko Marin became aware for the first time when he received the written order?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's possible if the chief of staff had not informed him about my oral order or the person who attended the team meeting. So it's possible that he personally learned about that task for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I want to use this time to ask you another question. When you came back to the team meeting on the 16th of April, when somebody spoke about the intensity of the fighting in Ahmici, somebody in that meeting spoke about the intensity of the combat; do you remember that you said that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That there was fierce combat activity, yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But did you know that you had HVO units in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Units of the military police, their commander informed me that he was in Ahmici in the morning at about 11.42 on the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: The intensity that somebody spoke about at the meeting on the 16th, didn't that jog curiosity, or perhaps your duty as a commander of the Operative Zone, to learn what the results of the combat -- of the static combat that you mentioned were? So that on the 16th, you learned that there had been intense fighting. On the 17th, 18th, 19th, 20th, 21st, did you never ask what the results of such intense fighting were?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not only had I asked but I asked for written information, to receive written information, to get specific reports about the outcome, the results of all the fighting, and I tried to get information because there wasn't only fighting in Ahmici but in 20 other places as well. So there was intense fighting in other places, including the hotel which was hit that morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you, General. I'm trying to be as direct as possible so we don't use up too much time. But when you said, "Not only did I ask, but I asked for written reports," I think that you're saying that you made an oral request and a written request. That's what I've understood.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was in touch with the commanders, in telephone touch, and I asked for information and reports about the events in Busovaca and Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: When, for the first time after the 16th, or maybe even on the 16th, after having spoken about the intensity of the fighting, when did you ask for information about the results of the fighting?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't remember precisely, but my demands and requests for information and reports, it's all there in my chronology. It was minute-by-minute information. The telephone was ringing every five minutes about the outcome, the result, the intensity, and all the other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, General. I can understand your answer. But for a commander of an operative zone, when somebody says that there was intense fighting on the 16th, it seems natural to me to try to find out on the same day or the next day or would you only find out about what happened a month later?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, at that time, combat was going on, and it was presented here, combat was going on in 22 places, intense fighting in 22 places, total encirclement in 22 places. I did everything that I could in order to receive as complete information as possible, and even at that time, I asked for specific and complete information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let me give the floor to Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit D280, which represents a written report from Ahmici which arrived on the 16th of April, 1993, General, except that written report, did you receive oral reports in the course of the day about the combat in Ahmici? Before that report, did you receive oral reports about the fighting in Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. The first report I received was at 11.42 on the 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, did you receive further oral reports about the events in Ahmici from Commander Pasko Ljubicic by telephone?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask for written reports as well, besides that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, and you can see that from this document, D220, where he cites the order that I issued, and also, in subsequent days, I did not only issue orders but warnings that I had to have complete and true information about the events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the 16th of April, out of all the numerous oral reports and from this written report, did information reach you from anywhere that a crime had been committed in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another thing. The documents, the orders that you issued of any kind, do they automatically go to the operations and training department or is this specific only for some orders or is this a matter of routine?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it's a matter of routine. All orders go there because one person has the task of recording and also monitoring the deadlines for the implementation of the orders. I would sign over 400 orders a month, and I couldn't monitor all of them, and that is why there was a person in the operations and training department who used to record the orders and monitor their implementation. He would possibly remind those who were supposed to implement the orders about the deadline for the implementation of that order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So sending all orders to the operations and training department, did that have anything to do -- whether it had to do with combat or administration matters?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. This was strictly an administrative procedure and it had nothing to do with any kind of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oral orders for investigations and the written orders for investigations in the case of Ahmici, were they given to one in the same person?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The weight of an oral and a written order, is it the same or is it different? Must they be implemented?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's the same. It has to be implemented. As far as a soldier is concerned, there is no difference there. Both of them have the same weight, the same value.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the completion of the investigation, when the SIS commander, head of SIS, Ante Sliskovic, told you that the file was sent to Mostar on orders, could you, did you have the legal authority, to order him to act differently?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. The priority, precisely because of the dual chain of command, his priority as a superior, the head of SIS in Mostar, these were priority tasks, and regardless of what I ordered, he had to act in accordance with the tasks that he received from his superiors. I was not authorised nor did I have the legal option of changing that decision or that task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the head of SIS, Ante Sliskovic, told you that he received an order from his superiors for the investigation files regarding Ahmici be sent to Mostar, so to higher military command, what did you believe would happen at that time? What did you believe would happen?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that time, I believed that the authorised persons from the SIS administration will continue to process this and that the military top command would carry out the processing and they would deal with those suspected of committing the war crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you think that the military command would end this investigation in a better or worse way than you would?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, better, of course, because their powers were greater and there was a need to detain a larger number of suspects, and obviously my command power at that time was much smaller.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After receiving the news that the file was sent to Mostar, did you receive any signals or indications based on which you could conclude that something positive or negative was happening? Did you see anything which would point to you that something was happening?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I received information that high officials from the SIS administration on two occasions, in October and November, they went and made the final controls of the results of the investigations, and I believed that they would carry on with the prosecution of the suspects.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you believe, that there would be court proceedings in Vitez, in Mostar? Did you think about that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believed that the only possible and the surest way would be to hold the trial in Mostar due to the overall situation that was prevalent in the area of Vitez at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Parallel with the investigation, which was obviously completed, did you take any measures to prevent those who had taken part in the crime in Ahmici, the military police, that they do not repeat such a crime? I'm talking about especially prevention with regard to military police, and if so, what was that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, in the conditions of total encirclement, in a situation that had no way out, I spent a lot of time, first of all, to effect a change in the command structure within the military police, and then with Mr. Palavra, who in the former army was a plain soldier, to work to enable him and to enable his command to carry out very large changes in the structure, especially regarding those who were subject to punishment in the military police. I was trying -- my attempts to have those persons dismissed from the military police were not fruitful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that whole period, did you ever find any single name or had any proof that any person had committed a crime in Ahmici? Do you have any single names?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you then initiate disciplinary proceedings?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, because the biggest problem was the problem of getting the names of the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you something now about something that we did not discuss in the course of this trial and that I believe is significant. Could you please explain to the Court what atmosphere or how did public opinion, among the army and the people in these enclaves on the model, what was the public opinion regarding the crime that was committed in Ahmici in 1993? If you could please tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, there were objective problems and difficulties, naturally. If only Ahmici had happened, I believe that there would have been general condemnation by all of those who lived -- all of the peoples, the citizens, who lived in that area, and that there would have been general support for this crime to be investigated and to be wholly processed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber, I think this is important, did the public support an investigation or not? And you requested the investigation.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why didn't it? Could you please explain that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were a lot of reasons. I already said that. I think that one of the reasons was, of course, that this was not the first crime that happened, crimes had happened before, but it seemed to the public that some had an exclusive right for information to be published and to sacrifice while the others did not. There was a large number of refugees and they kept arriving daily, and I said that there were about 35.000 people. These were desperate people who were forced to watch from that enclave how their houses were burned down every day. They pulled out at the same time as the HVO troops pulled out, under pressure of the B and H army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these refugees contribute towards a positive or a negative attitude towards the investigation of the Ahmici case?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it was negative. If we take that the total number, 70.000 population in the enclave, including the 35.000 refugees, so then we would have 50 per cent of desperate people, the rest would be the local population, and, of course, these were desperate people. They mainly came just carrying a little bag in their hand. Recently, I was watching refugees from Kosovo that were coming on tractors. I don't remember seeing anybody who managed to come with a tractor or on a truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What else had an effect to radicalise the situation and create resistance towards an investigation of the Ahmici case?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, there were a lot of children and older people and victims of, most often, sniper activity and shelling, including activities by tanks in town, such as Busovaca and Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to these children?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The children were killed by snipers and by mortar shells, so this also made the situation more radical. Children were also wounded. There were cases where a whole family was wiped out. We had 80 children who did not have either both parents or did not have a mother or a father, one of the parents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many were there killed in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was about 1.300 soldiers and the total number of casualties was around 2.000, and only in the area of Vitez, there were 650 soldiers killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, it's a long morning. Ordinarily, we take two breaks. Do you want to ask another question on that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just one question in order to round this off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In spite of this situation and your efforts to have an investigation, did anybody seriously support your efforts to carry out an investigation about Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Apart from my own personal efforts and the efforts made by the security officials, there wasn't any support, I did not feel anybody's support, and even more so because the struggle for survival went on for almost a year in that area and there was not a single safe position; that is to say, when a soldier was not in a trench, he knew that there was not a single safe place where he could rest even for an hour. The question was for how long we could survive and how long we could endure in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We can take a break at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think we will take a 20-minute break. It's been a long morning and we're all beginning to get tired. We'll start at about a quarter after twelve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. I am convinced that the Judges' questions have moved you forward, Mr. Nobilo, so that you can finish by 1.30. I'm convinced of that. Now let me reassure you that if it isn't finished, we will take that time necessary when Judge Shahabuddeen comes back. We want things to be very clear. You have to carry out your mission; we have to carry out ours as completely as possible. If you finish, all the better; if you don't, we'll continue at another time, because we interrupted you. Mr. Nobilo, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you for your understanding, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, on several occasions, the Prosecutor put rhetorical questions to you. "Give us at least one name of a person who was punished for this or that offence." So could you please explain to the Court how you, as commander of the Operative Zone, viewed your role in the process of punishing the perpetrators of crimes?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I issued clear instructions and orders to my subordinates that I would not tolerate the commission of crimes, and my positions were quite clear in that respect and I should say that they were generally known to all my associates. If, after the investigation, I would receive information about the perpetrators of crimes, I would also act in accordance with a system: I would either file a criminal report or I would ask the competent authorities to do that through the district military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you think that, as commander of the Operative Zone, it was your duty to personally conduct investigations of individual crimes?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not think that was my duty, and it was not at that level where it was possible for me to do so either. I tried to work in accordance with a system and to make sure that a system be established that would function and where competent expert professionals would carry out investigations and also initiate proceedings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your schooling, did you receive any training as an investigator of crime?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. In the former JNA and also in the HVO, I always tried to make sure that the system operated and that everyone, in keeping with his own abilities and legal responsibilities, carries out his duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the case of prosecuting criminal offences, what was the most important thing and what was the most difficult thing?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The most difficult thing was to discover the perpetrators of criminal offences, that is to say, to arrive at the name and surname of the perpetrator of a crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, in keeping with the decree on armed forces and other laws, which bodies did you have at your disposal that did have the power to investigate crime?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The military police and the security service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What could you do in respect of criminal offences? What could you do and what could you ask the security service and the military police to do?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I could request that they be engaged in the efforts aimed at discovering the perpetrators of criminal offences. However, I already said that due to the dual change of command, the orders of their direct superiors from Mostar always had priority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you issue orders to these organs and did you ask in that way to investigate the perpetrators of all crimes, including war crimes?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did that and I insisted on that, and sometimes I would even repeat orders and sometimes I would issue orders in respect of orders, and I would inform my superiors about all the problems that I was facing in such activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether they, within their own hierarchy, received the same kind of orders from their superiors? Do you know what kind of orders they received from their superiors?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of orders they received. In that sense, they were quite autonomous and independent of me, in that respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree with the assertion that the military police is the biggest, and then there is SIS also, that they were inefficient in investigating crimes in the Lasva River Valley in 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When a body is inefficient, could you have changed the structure of the military police or of the SIS?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not have such powers, and I could only repeat my requests, my insistence, and I would write and ask that the structure of the establishment of the HVO be changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you cannot change the bodies that are supposed to discover the perpetrators of crimes and they don't do that well, what could you do in that situation?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The only thing I could do in that situation -- or, rather, I could not punish anyone. I could only ask for the structure, the organisational structure, to be changed, primarily of the military police, so that later I would manage to achieve changes within the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you came to the conclusion that -- the organ that is supposed to discover crimes, did you reconcile yourself to that or did you try to do something and did you manage to do something? Tell the Court about that.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not reconcile myself to that, and I insisted that the structure of the establishment of the military police be changed. And already from August 1993, thanks to the appointment of Palavra as head of the military police, I managed, together with him, within a very short period of time, to achieve changes in the military police, to train it to the extent to which this was possible under those circumstances, and thus perpetrators of crimes were discovered more easily but also public law and order were enhanced and also crime suppression was improved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember a name, a single name of a single case when the military police or SIS gave you the name of a perpetrator and that you did not take disciplinary action or that you did not ask for criminal proceedings to be initiated?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was certainly no such case. There was not a single case that I received a name and surname and that I did not react, either in terms of criminal proceedings or in terms of disciplinary proceedings, and this was generally known not only to the members of my command but also to my immediate associates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My colleague, the Prosecutor, had been cross-examining you for weeks and this trial has been going on for two years. Do you remember a single piece of evidence that was presented to this Court on the basis of which we could conclude that you found out who the perpetrators of a crime were and that you did not want to initiate proceedings against such a person? Is there any such evidence?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please, could this group of exhibits that we have prepared, these are Defence Exhibits, could they please be shown? We are not going to read all of them. We would just like to see D220, D219, D221, D222, D223, D224, D225, D226, D227, D228, D229, D230, D231, D232, D233, D234.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just take a quick look at this? Could you please give him all the documents so that he could see them all very quickly? And could you please tell the Court what these documents are and what they prove? All together, not one paper by one paper, one document by one document, all together what do these documents show?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: All these documents show that there were accurate records about the disciplinary measures that were pronounced, about disciplinary punishment that was taken, that is to say, that if measures were pronounced, that the sentence had to be served and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: For the method here, I'd like to make two comments. I would like to congratulate the rapidity with which the General is able to familiarise himself with the documents, that's different than what it was in the past, and you have to admit that the Judges don't have the documents in front of them. So we're listening to the witness who is saying what he wants to say, but there has to be a method. I know it's a little longer. We don't have to look at all the details of the documents, but at least let us define the documents, whether it be either Mr. Nobilo or the witness, at least give us the number of the document that you're talking about; otherwise, it's really simply an argument and your client is saying what he wants to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We have enumerated the documents and they are in the transcript, and they just show how intensively disciplinary proceedings were carried out. We just wanted to recall that. We don't want to go into each and every document, but we just wanted to put together in one place all the documents that speak of disciplinary proceedings that were taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is your right, and I think it's a good method to make a comment, you, the Defence attorneys, but not to have your client say "This document proves this or that." We couldn't use that kind of method. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more question related to disciplinary proceedings. The Prosecutor quoted Article 29 to you from the decree on disciplinary action, that is to say, that even when criminal proceedings are initiated, that you are authorised to take disciplinary proceedings, and you said that you didn't do that. Why? Could you explain this to the Court?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Theoretically, this was possible, and practically, if it was established that a soldier had committed a criminal offence, on the instructions of the district military prosecutor, he was put into the investigative prison, investigative military prison, and then an investigation was started, and then he would receive a sentence, one to five years of imprisonment, I can't remember the exact range, and the maximum that he could get in disciplinary proceedings would be up to 60 days of military detention. So from a practical point of view, it was not exactly expedient, because this soldier, if he was the perpetrator of a criminal offence, he had even previously been removed from a unit and his issued weapons were taken away from him, and he would be prosecuted by the district military prosecutor for the commission of a crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, what were your possibilities -- what was your authority in criminal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, if I would receive the names of the perpetrator of a criminal offence, that is to say, if the military police service or the security service provide me with the names of the perpetrator of a crime, I could file a criminal report against that perpetrator, and I did file criminal reports against perpetrators of crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who decided whether criminal proceedings would be instituted or not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was exclusively within the authority of the military district prosecutor. I did not have any authority in that respect. I could not influence the decision of the district military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now a few words about the authority of the civilian and military police. Can you tell us how this authority was exercised? When was the civilian police in charge and when was the military police in charge?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If the perpetrator of a crime was a civilian, then the investigation was carried out by the civilian police; if the perpetrator of a crime was a soldier, then the investigation was carried out by the military police; and if the perpetrator of a crime was unknown, then the investigation was carried by the authorities of the civilian police force. They would establish a file and they would work until it was established, possibly, that the perpetrator was a military man, and then the entire file would be handed over to the military police for their further processing. But it is primarily the civilian police that carried out on-site investigations and carried out the investigation in general if the perpetrator was unknown.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In respect of criminal investigations of the civilian police, did you have any authority in that respect?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. There was an entire system of the civilian police. They had their own commander, they had their own superior, so to speak, and I did not have any authority over the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the administration of the civilian police? Did it function throughout the war in the enclave where you were, in the Lasva River Valley?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the administration was in charge of all of Central Bosnia and it functioned in Travnik until the fall of Travnik and later it was moved to Vitez, and it was in charge of all the police stations within the territory of Central Bosnia, all civilian police stations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything change in the powers of the civilian and military police over civilian and military persons because there was a war going on, in respect of war and peace?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, now we would like to move on to a different area, that is, whether the conflict was international or internal, this is a matter that the Court will certainly be interested in, and the Prosecutor presented here as evidence an entire series of orders issued by Croatian General Bobetko, and, therefore, we would like to look into this very important area now. Could the Judges and the witness please be given the following documents: Defence Exhibit (sic) 406/6, 406/7, 406/8, 406/9, 406/10, 406/11, 406/12, 406/13, 406/14, 406/15, 406/16, 406/19, 406/20, 406/21, 406/22. Prosecutor's Exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Wasn't that indicated before, Mr. Registrar? It's taking quite a lot of time here. It's taking a long time.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, would you take a quick look at these documents? Don't read through them all, we aren't going to discuss them in detail, but just look at the dates. Take a look at the dates to see when they were issued and make a note of the earliest date and the latest date, please. Well, General, have you taken a look at the documents, General Bobetko's documents, his orders and the other documents from his book, and what time span are they?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: According to the documents that I received, April, May, and June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, do you know General Bobetko?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do know General Bobetko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you read his book?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've read his book.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask a document to be passed round before the rest.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D574 and D574A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We haven't got the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You haven't?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The usher has gone to make a copy for the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, General, according to the best of your knowledge, in reading General Bobetko's books and according to your general knowledge, why did General Bobetko, with the troops of the Croatian army, enter the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Quite obviously he had a goal and an assignment, that is to say, to stop the invasion of the southern portion of Croatia, above all, Dubrovnik and Split, and to stabilise the defence on a broad base, so as to create the prerequisites necessary to stop a complete occupation, to prevent a complete occupation. And he entered Bosnia-Herzegovina with his troops in order to have the necessary operative depth in which to develop and deploy the HVO units in the defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did he enter into conflict with? Who was included into that armed conflict during the time that General Bobetko was located in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the one side, in that part, we had the Croatian army, supported by local Croats and Muslims, and on the other side, there were the members of the Yugoslav People's Army, or the Yugoslav army as it was called at the time, supported by the local Serbs who the Yugoslav army had mobilised into its composition, into its ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask that the map be distributed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D575.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Does everybody have the maps? Does the Prosecutor have the maps? Let's try to move forward. I hope that the military breakthroughs of the army are more rapid than the distribution of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The maps are Defence Exhibits D575/1, D575/2, D575/3, and so on, in order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I should now like to ask you briefly to explain these maps to us. They are photocopies taken from General Bobetko's book, and as the map is in colour, the original map, I just used a marker to denote the positions of the Yugoslav army. So the colour you see in there are the front lines and the axes in which the Yugoslav army moved. I'd like to ask you to read out the title of the map, what it represents, and to tell us briefly what the map represents. So, first of all, read out the text on the first map, Defence Exhibit D575/1.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: And I'm reading the title: "The planned and implemented operations of the forces of the JNA and the Chetnik units," on the 10th of April, "10/04/1992. Legend: The focal points of Serb uprising, the axes of attack by the JNA forces, and the Chetnik units realised and those planned. The secret activities of the enemy."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you, because the map is not a very detailed one, indicate the borders of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina in the southern portion? Take up the pointer, please, to give an indication to the Court where the frontier of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina was.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The border was this dotted line (indicating), and it goes via Azan, Imotska, towards Vervovac, Capljina, Metkovic, Neum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, so in the south, it is right near the coastline. When you look at the arrows which indicate the axes of attack of the Yugoslav People's Army, what are you able to conclude? For them, the battleground in both states, is it a unified battleground, or are the combat operations conducted in such a fashion that they would have to take into account where the republican borders lay?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The battleground was treated as a unified whole, regardless of whether -- regardless of the republican borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, and that can be seen from the operations realised by the JNA in the valley of the River Neretva and in the region behind Dubrovnik, as well as in the north by the forces of the Knin Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which state is Knin in?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Knin is in the Republic of Croatia. And those forces were halted north-west of Livno, north of Livno as well, and north of Tomislavgrad, that is to say, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So those forces treated a uniform battleground from Split to Dubrovnik up until Kupres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, what were the JNA's plans, according to this deployment of forces? The JNA on the right-hand side of the map, did they want to join up with the JNA on the other side of the map, and had that occurred, what would that have meant?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At all events, the operations that were conducted in the Neretva valley, the delta of the River Neretva, moving towards the south and Dubrovnik, should have continued to the right bank of the River Neretva, and there we have the force -- this was done by the Herzegovina forces of the JNA, and the forces of the Knin Corps were contained in the existing positions and operations were to have continued along the general axis toward Sinj and to have a joining up of forces with the forces of the Herzegovina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had that joining up taken place, what would that have meant for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Had that joining of forces taken place, then that would have meant a complete occupation and encirclement of Bosnia-Herzegovina because the forces of the Herzegovinian corps would have come out at Ploce, and the Knin corps forces would have been about the town of Split itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it have been possible in that case to bring any logistics and the military materiel to the BH army and the HVO in Central Bosnia? Would that have been possible?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it would not have been possible. Not only would no logistics have been possible but the evacuation of refugees and aid and assistance generally would have been impossible because the pliers around Bosnia and Herzegovina would have been completely closed, the town of Livno towards Neum, and this would have been a completely occupied area. It wouldn't have been occupied 70 per cent, but Bosnia-Herzegovina would have been occupied 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we have a look at the next map after the 10th of April, when Croatian forces entered Bosnia-Herzegovina? Once again, we have a map copied from General Bobetko's book, and the pink denotes the forces of the Yugoslav army. Can you tell us what this map represents?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This map represents the attacks implemented by the forces of the Yugoslav army and the counterattack by the Croatian army in between the 23rd up until the 27th of April, 1992. In the legend, the legend states the first phase of the implementation of the assignments on the southern front, a successfully thwarted attack of the enemy with significant losses. Then it says "Counterattacks" and part of the territory lost fortifying the defence of HB, breaking down the enemy attack core, nucleus, and forcing the enemy to defend the occupied -- and it doesn't say what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us see, once again, who the conflicting sides are. Who fought against whom?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the side of the attacker, we have the forces of the Yugoslav army, and here we see that it was the 13th Partisan Brigade. Then we have the TO detachment of Ljubina and the TO of Danilovgrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the other side, who was on the other side?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the other side, we had the forces of the Croatian army ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We don't need to know the units, General. Let us take a look at the next map and look at the dates that this refers to.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This map shows the defence line of the southern battlefront on the 10th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is the front line before the breakthrough?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that was the front line before the attack by the Yugoslav army and the counterattack by the Croatian army, and you can see clearly from Mostar, along the Neretva River Valley, through Hutovo, that's the front line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we look at the next map, please?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This map shows the attacks by the Croatian army in the second stage of the implementation of the tasks on the southern front in the period from the 18th of May until the 30th of May, 1992. On one side, we have the forces of the Yugoslav army once again, helped with mobilised persons from Montenegro and other areas. On the other side, we have the forces of the HV.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at the next map?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This map shows the attacks by the Croatian army in deblocking Dubrovnik in the period from the 27th of May until the 19th of October, 1992, and on one side, we have forces of the Yugoslav army and on the other side are forces of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do we have another map? Let's look at the last map.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is a decision of the commander of the southern front, code name "Tiger," to carry out the liberation of Dubrovnik and the terrain right behind it. Forces of the Croatian army are participating in that action. On the other side, we have members of the Yugoslav army and mobilised Serbs and Montenegrins.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, could you please tell us how long General Bobetko was in Bosnia-Herzegovina with his troops? How long did the battle on the southern front last?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It lasted until October, I think, of '92, and after that, the HV forces and General Bobetko were transferred to another area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that period, from the 10th of April 1993 until October 1993, during the time General Bobetko and the Croatian army were in Bosnia and Herzegovina, was there a conflict between the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, meaning the TO, and the HV?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. They participated together in most of the actions, the Croatian forces and the Bosniak Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you explain the fact that in that time period, General Bobetko not only stayed with the Croatian troops in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but he was obviously, on HVO letterheads, issuing orders to certain groups of the HVO in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He issued orders by the very fact that neither the Territorial Defence nor the units of the HVO, they were not structured or organised at that time, and earlier, I had a document in my hands where he issued an order, that's document 574, where he says in item 2, he orders units of the Territorial Defence, it's headed to the general staff in Hrvatska Grude, and then it also includes units of the Territorial Defence. Neither the Territorial Defence nor the HVO were structured. This was not completed. They mostly were active at the level of municipalities under the crisis committees, the crisis staffs. They were only beginning to get organised at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Court when the law was adopted, the law on the armed forces, which was the basis for the organisation of the HVO as an army?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This was done at the beginning of July 1992, I think it happened on the 3rd of July, 1992, and only in the second half of August of '92 were the officers named for the defence department of the HVO, which later grew into the Defence Ministry as a body which would be in charge of creating and organising the military structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, as an expert, at the time that General Bobetko and the Croatian troops were in Herzegovina, did the HVO exist at all as an organised armed force?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. These were local groups, and only the beginnings, the first attempts to structure these groups were being made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I would like the usher to distribute a new document and to give it a number, a new exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be D576, D576A for the English version. Let me say that the previous document, that is, the maps, that was 575/1, 2, up to 6. There were six maps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to read parts of the letter by General Bobetko to Franjo Tudjman which were published on pages 137 and 138 of his book. The letter is addressed to the president of the republic, Franjo Tudjman: "Mr. President, the offensive operations on the southern front of the Croatian Army forces, numbering 1.475 soldiers, have begun on July 1st 1992. Until July 5th 1992, the following results were achieved," and then the results are enumerated. At the end, the assessment right at the end of the letter: "I assess that this is one of the most difficult attacks, one of the toughest attacks I had on this front. I take it that it has been performed well. We have created conditions for final liberation of this part of Croatian territory. "Sincerely, Commander of the Southern Front Army, General Janko Bobetko, Dubrovnik, July 5th 1992."

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I made a mistake. I saw that operations were completed in July, and I think I stated that they had been completed in October of 1992. But Konavle and the rear was liberated, and that was completed in October.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could we look at the next document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D577, D577A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We translated only the section that was marked, that was highlighted, so I'm going to read that, and then I will ask you a question, General. This is a photocopy of page 267 from General Bobetko's book. He is talking about the results of the Croatian army: "Number one, we have managed to defend and preserve for good the existence of Croatian people in Herzegovina. "Number two, we have created favourable circumstances in order to establish an army. In the context of events that go on these days regarding the forming of the federation and the confederation, it stands to question what our position would be" without these victories, what would that mean for our international as well as local position? "The operation itself has created very favourable operative conditions for final operations on the southern front, the main purpose of which is to expel the Montenegrin aggressor and to deploy forces to the area of Prevlaka," meaning to deblock Dubrovnik, "... and reclaiming the entire territory which has been under enemy occupation for over two years, and which has been considered by the enemy to be the final solution for borders of Great Serbia in these areas." General, General Bobetko states that these actions that you have just talked about which we showed on the maps, among other things, created favourable conditions to create an army of the future federation. How do you interpret that, and is that consistent with what you know about those operations?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I interpret that to mean that these actions prevented the complete occupation of the only territory through which Bosnia and Herzegovina could receive any kind of help and that conditions were created to organise both the HVO and the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and, in some way, to continue with the process of the structuring of the federal army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we conclude from that, what you stated earlier, that there was no HVO army at that time when the Croatian army entered the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. These were mostly armed formations or several armed formations which were managed by municipal crisis staffs. There were no brigades. There was no order on the creation of armed forces. There was no law. There was no formal defence department at that time. In some documents, the general staff is mentioned, but what they meant by that was mostly the administration, the administrative tasks in order to create an army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The relationships that are evident from Prosecution Exhibits, which are orders of General Bobetko illustrating relations between the HV and the HVO in April, May, and June of 1992, are these relationships, according to your knowledge, contained in the second half of '92 and went on into '93, the relationship of superiority and subordination?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. It will be clear, if you look at the book of General Bobetko, that after the final operations and the liberation of Dubrovnik and the Dubrovnik hinterlands, he withdrew, and there was a regrouping of those forces and that there was no more -- such relationship no longer existed, but the HVO structured itself and was organised just like the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I would like to look at another document. It's also a copy from General Bobetko's book, it's page 419. Mr. President, I still have two questions on this document, and then after that, we can stop, or do you believe that we need to break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You won't be finished this morning then?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No. I don't have more than 20 or 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You still have another 30 minutes. All right. Then we'll start again when Judge Shahabuddeen returns. We said that we would take advantage of having Mr. Fourmy here for a few moments so that we can see what the schedule is going to be for next week and the week after that. I don't know whether it's Mr. Fourmy or Mr. Hayman who can give us clarification for next week, during which ordinarily we should sit in a bench accepted by the Defence pursuant to Rule 71 but conditional on there being a witness, which is not perhaps certain. Mr. Hayman, perhaps you could shed some light on that issue for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, we don't have any more information about the witnesses that we were trying to get here on Monday, and because we think they will be short, we would request that we keep them as a block and that we not plan on hearing them next week but we'll slot them in when the Court indicates. We think half a day will be sufficient for the three "sentencing phase" witnesses. Again, we apologise for the disorganisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, all of us have problems with witnesses that we have to bring in, especially given the context of what's going on now. Let me turn to Mr. Fourmy and then I'll hear what the Prosecutor has to say. Mr. Fourmy, I suppose that you've contacted the appropriate people. Are you going on vacation or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: Well, I would be very pleased to suggest that the Trial Chamber take advantage of the time when Judge Shahabuddeen will not be here for the other two Judges and the parties to have a free week next week, which would allow the Defence to use the time to verify where things stand for the three witnesses. The following week, we can bring in the witnesses depending upon their availability; that is, the Trial Chamber's witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Therefore, I understand, Mr. Hayman, that you think that your three witnesses will be available not next week but the week after that, which would allow us to sit in a full bench, which, of course, would be a good thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we suggest that our three witnesses be heard on the 7th of June. We could hear them all on the afternoon of the 7th of June without any problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Monday, the 7th of June. All right. There's no problem with that. That would give us the opportunity to use next week. We had thought about bringing in some of the Trial Chamber's witnesses next week and we had hoped you would make contact with those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: We are trying to find out whether four of the witnesses will come during the week of the 7th to the 11th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Next week, Judge Rodrigues and I will devote our time to other cases before the Trial Chamber. We know that Judge Shahabuddeen will be in Arusha with the Appeals Chamber. Now I suggest that we adjourn, unless the Prosecutor has any comments to make about that schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, we're satisfied with the schedule. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If everybody's satisfied, we will adjourn, and I will see you during the week of the 7th of June. Thank you very much. The court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 1.29 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 7th day of June, 1999, at 2.00 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
